title: What is GraphX — Spark's API for graph-parallel computation (vertices + edges as RDDs, supports PageRank, connected components, triangle counting) — and what is MLlib — Spark's machine learning library (classification, regression, clustering, recommendation, feature engineering via Pipeline API)?

s1_definition.profdef: GraphX is Spark's library for graph-parallel computation, representing a graph as a distributed set of vertices and edges backed by RDDs, and providing graph algorithms such as PageRank for influence ranking, connected components for finding clusters of linked nodes, and triangle counting for measuring local connectivity. MLlib is Spark's distributed machine learning library, offering algorithms for classification, regression, clustering, and recommendation, plus feature engineering and a high-level Pipeline API built on DataFrames that chains feature transformers and estimators into a single reproducible workflow with fit and transform semantics. Both run on the Spark engine so they scale the same distributed computation to large datasets across a cluster.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India GraphX is the tool for questions about relationships — who sends money to whom. If you draw every account as a dot and every transfer as an arrow between dots, GraphX can find rings of accounts that all move money among themselves (connected components), rank which accounts are most central to the money flow (PageRank), and spot tight triangles of mutual transfers that may signal collusion (triangle counting). MLlib is the tool for learning from data — training a model on past transactions to predict which new ones are likely fraudulent (classification), grouping customers by behaviour (clustering), or recommending products — and its Pipeline API is like a fixed assembly line that cleans and prepares the data and then runs the model, the same way every time.
s1_definition.oneliner: GraphX does graph-parallel computation on vertices and edges (PageRank, connected components, triangle counting); MLlib does distributed machine learning (classification, regression, clustering, recommendation) with a DataFrame-based Pipeline API for feature engineering and models.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** GraphX is Spark's library for graph-parallel computation, representing a graph as a distributed set of vertices and edges backed by RDDs, and providing graph algorithms such as PageRank for influence ranking, connected components for finding clusters of linked nodes, and triangle counting for measuring local connectivity. MLlib is Spark's distributed machine learning library, offering algorithms for classification, regression, clustering, and recommendation, plus feature engineering and a high-level Pipeline API built on DataFrames that chains feature transformers and estimators into a single reproducible workflow with fit and transform semantics. Both run on the Spark engine so they scale the same distributed computation to large datasets across a cluster.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India GraphX is the tool for questions about relationships — who sends money to whom. If you draw every account as a dot and every transfer as an arrow between dots, GraphX can find rings of accounts that all move money among themselves (connected components), rank which accounts are most central to the money flow (PageRank), and spot tight triangles of mutual transfers that may signal collusion (triangle counting). MLlib is the tool for learning from data — training a model on past transactions to predict which new ones are likely fraudulent (classification), grouping customers by behaviour (clustering), or recommending products — and its Pipeline API is like a fixed assembly line that cleans and prepares the data and then runs the model, the same way every time.

**One line to remember:** GraphX does graph-parallel computation on vertices and edges (PageRank, connected components, triangle counting); MLlib does distributed machine learning (classification, regression, clustering, recommendation) with a DataFrame-based Pipeline API for feature engineering and models.

sections.s2_technical:
GraphX models a graph as two distributed collections: a vertex RDD of node identifiers with attributes, and an edge RDD of source-to-destination pairs with attributes, combined into a Graph abstraction. On top of this it offers a graph-parallel computation model — notably the Pregel API, where computation proceeds in supersteps as vertices exchange messages along edges — and a set of ready-made algorithms. PageRank scores each vertex by how important the vertices linking to it are, which surfaces central nodes. Connected components labels each vertex with the id of the cluster it belongs to, grouping nodes reachable from one another. Triangle counting counts how many triangles each vertex participates in, a measure of local density. GraphX is powerful for relationship analytics, though in newer Spark the DataFrame-based GraphFrames library is often preferred for its richer query API.

MLlib provides the standard families of machine learning. Classification predicts a category, such as fraud or not fraud, with algorithms like logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, and gradient-boosted trees. Regression predicts a continuous number, such as an expected transaction amount. Clustering groups unlabeled data, for example k-means to segment customers. Recommendation uses collaborative filtering, such as alternating least squares, to suggest products. These algorithms are implemented to run distributed across the cluster, so they train on datasets far larger than one machine's memory.

Feature engineering and the Pipeline API are central to MLlib's modern usage. Raw data must be turned into numeric feature vectors, so MLlib provides transformers like StringIndexer to encode categories, OneHotEncoder, VectorAssembler to combine columns into a single features vector, and scalers for normalization. The Pipeline API, built on DataFrames, chains these transformers and a final estimator into one object. A Pipeline has fit, which learns any needed statistics and trains the model producing a PipelineModel, and the PipelineModel has transform, which applies the whole sequence to new data. This makes the preprocessing and the model a single reproducible unit, which prevents training-serving skew where the preprocessing differs between training and prediction.

The two libraries fit different problem shapes and are sometimes combined. GraphX answers questions about connectivity and influence in a network, while MLlib answers predictive and grouping questions from tabular features. In fraud detection they often work together: GraphX or GraphFrames extracts graph features like an account's PageRank or its connected-component size, and those features are fed into an MLlib classifier that predicts fraud. A senior-level nuance is knowing the ecosystem direction and the limits: GraphX is RDD-based and somewhat legacy, with GraphFrames preferred for new work, and MLlib's older RDD-based API is deprecated in favour of the DataFrame-based spark.ml package, so you build pipelines with spark.ml. You also recognize that Spark MLlib targets large-scale distributed training of classical algorithms rather than deep learning, for which you would integrate a dedicated framework. The mature answer is to use GraphX or GraphFrames for relationship analytics, spark.ml pipelines for scalable classical machine learning with reproducible feature engineering, and to combine them when network structure is a useful predictive signal.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to find rings of accounts that transfer money among themselves, which is a connected-components problem on the transfer graph, a GraphX use case.

Problem 2 — The bank wants to predict whether a new transaction is fraudulent from features like amount and channel, which is a classification problem solved by an MLlib pipeline.

Problem 3 — The graph structure is itself a useful signal, so the size of an account's connected component becomes a feature fed into the classifier, combining GraphX and MLlib.

The demo simulates both: a tiny connected-components computation over a transfer graph to label account rings, and a tiny rule-based stand-in for an MLlib pipeline that assembles features (including the component size) and produces a fraud score, logging the graph labels and the predictions.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer graph with a four-account ring A to B to C to D back to A, plus an isolated pair SAV2001 to CUR3001.

Step 1: Connected components runs over the edges using union-find. The four ring accounts are merged into one component, and the pair forms a separate component. Each account is labeled with its component id, the GraphX-style result.

Step 2: Component sizes are computed. Account A's component has size four (the ring), and SAV2001's component has size two (the pair). This graph structure becomes a feature.

Step 3: The MLlib-style pipeline scores a high-value transaction on an unknown channel inside the four-account ring. The amount signal, the unknown-channel signal, and the large-component signal all fire, producing a high fraud score near one.

Step 4: The pipeline scores a normal small transaction in the pair. None of the risk signals fire strongly, producing a low score. The demo logs the component sizes and both scores, showing GraphX output feeding an MLlib-style prediction.

sections.s6_takeaway:
GraphX is Spark's library for graph-parallel computation. It represents a graph as a distributed vertex collection and edge collection backed by RDDs, combined into a Graph abstraction, and it offers a graph-parallel model including the Pregel message-passing API plus ready-made algorithms: PageRank to rank vertices by the importance of those linking to them, connected components to label clusters of mutually reachable nodes, and triangle counting to measure local connectivity. It answers questions about relationships and influence in a network, which in banking means things like finding rings of accounts that move money among themselves.

MLlib is Spark's distributed machine learning library. It provides the standard families — classification, regression, clustering, and recommendation — implemented to train across a cluster on data larger than one machine. Its modern core is the DataFrame-based spark.ml Pipeline API, which chains feature transformers like StringIndexer and VectorAssembler with a final estimator into one object that you fit to produce a model and then transform on new data. That makes preprocessing and the model a single reproducible unit, which is important because it prevents training-serving skew where the feature preparation differs between training and prediction.

At the National Bank of India these worked together in fraud detection. We used connected components on the transfer graph to find rings of collusive accounts, and the size of an account's connected component became a feature fed into an MLlib classification pipeline that predicted fraud from amount, channel, and that graph signal, so a high-value transaction on an unknown channel inside a tight ring scored much higher than a normal transaction in an isolated pair. The ecosystem nuances I mention in interviews are that GraphX is RDD-based and somewhat legacy with GraphFrames preferred for new graph work, that MLlib's older RDD API is deprecated in favour of the DataFrame-based spark.ml package, and that Spark MLlib targets large-scale classical algorithms rather than deep learning. The summary I give is: GraphX or GraphFrames for relationship analytics, spark.ml pipelines for scalable classical machine learning with reproducible feature engineering, and combine them when network structure is a useful predictive signal.
